newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Kohl wants EMU in 1999, but strict criteria.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kohl wants EMU in 1999, but strict criteria.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl said in an article published on Tuesday that European monetary union (EMU) should start on time in 1999, but that Germany would not allow a softening of the Maastricht criteria to meet that timetable.
"We want the euro to come punctually on January 1, 1999," Kohl wrote in the Deutsche Sparkassenzeitung. "But it is clear that this must not be at the expense of monetary stability."
Kohl added that European countries bore their own responsibility for achieving full convergence: "The stability criteria of the Maastricht treaty are not open to discussion."

Kohl's remarks come as doubts are mounting that Germany itself can meet the Maastricht budget deficit target of three percent of GDP which Bonn insists must be strictly adhered to for the launch of the euro currency to take place.

Hampered by a weak economy, record post-war unemployment and slack tax revenues, Finance Minister Theo Waigel has said welfare cuts and even tax increases could be needed this year to achieve the deficit target with room to spare.
In a separate interview with the Die Zeit weekly, Kohl's heir-apparent Wolfgang Schaeuble said that fulfilling the convergence criteria was "an absolute priority" for Germany.
Schaeuble, who is parliamentary leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), also said he strongly opposed a delay to European monetary union (EMU).

"We must fulfil the criteria, so that we do not have to postpone the euro. It is doubtful whether Europe would get a second chance after a delay," Schaeuble said in an interview released ahead of publication on Thursday.

Noting that the German public was sceptical towards EMU, he added: "If we do not hold to the three percent limit on the budget deficit, even this strong government will not have enough power to push through the euro."
Germany's insistence on a strict reading of Maastricht is widely seen as a way to exclude countries which do not have a long-term record of monetary stability and fiscal prudence.
Schaeuble said that if Germany gave up its position, monetary union could go out of control.

"If we all of a sudden abandon a strict interpretation, then we would no longer have control. For me there is barely a greater evil in economic, financial and social policy than not achieving the three percent," he told Die Zeit.
"We have to achieve something of which we are convinced. We also know that it worries a majority (of Germans). We must not reinforce those fears by softening the criteria."
